<reason>Both sides were sharp, disciplined, and honest under pressure, but A built the more durable route to victory. A's debt-versus-deletion asymmetry survived every attack: B's best counter ("an unpaid childhood is as irreversible") elevates a contingent compensation failure to parity with certain permanent loss, and A showed compensation can be bundled with and funded by regulation while extinct species and collapsed peat domes admit no compensation at all. A also answered B's pressure questions directly and specifically (naming the losers: undeveloped concessions and frontier conversion), then turned B's own "costless standard" into a liability — no polluter anywhere gets to keep harming until transition is guaranteed. Decisively, A's closing crystallized the clash B never resolved: B's entire alternative (prosecutions, fire brigades, damages) is ex-post, while the irreversible harms flow from lawful clearing at the moment a license is signed, which only ex-ante rules reach. B's "peat and primary forest are already banned" answer left lawful concession conversion and secondary-forest loss unaddressed. Two flaws cost A: its closing misdescribed B4.2 as "never answered" when B did offer damages/care, and biting "the rule stands even without compensation" was expensive. B fought back hard with motion fidelity, a clean enforcement/tightening distinction, and superb lines, but its clipped first rebuttal and its increasingly asserted premise that remaining legal expansion is harmless left A's prevention route live.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1 catch that B's closing prescription (enforce bans, title land, raise yields) is itself aggressive regulation set up the decisive thread; it matured in A's closing into the unanswered point that B's enforcement-and-damages toolkit is backward-looking and cannot prevent the permanent losses that occur through lawful clearing when licenses are signed.</best_rebuttal>
